query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: The accelerated coupled degradation of a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature is primarily caused by the synergistic effects of galvanic corrosion and oxidative wear, which are exacerbated by the formation of a dual-phase microstructure comprising a face-centered cubic (FCC) matrix and a sigma (σ) phase.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy with a dual-phase microstructure comprising a face-centered cubic (FCC) matrix and a sigma (σ) phase
generation.intervention: Exposure to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature, simultaneous wear and corrosion
generation.structural_mediator: Dual-phase microstructure comprising a face-centered cubic (FCC) matrix and a sigma (σ) phase
generation.predicted_outcome: A 30% increase in total degradation, with a 25% increase in wear rate and a 20% increase in corrosion current density, relative to a matched baseline
generation.baseline: Single-phase high-entropy alloy with a face-centered cubic (FCC) structure
generation.boundary: Elevated temperature range of 500-700°C, wear rate range of 10^-5 to 10^-4 mm^3/N·m, and corrosion current density range of 10^-4 to 10^-3 A/cm^2
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the synergistic effects of galvanic corrosion and oxidative wear on the coupled degradation of the multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy is uncertain and requires further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled comparison of the degradation behavior of a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy and a single-phase high-entropy alloy with a face-centered cubic (FCC) structure, exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the total degradation of the multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy is not significantly higher than that of the single-phase high-entropy alloy, with a threshold of 10% difference, then the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThis work studies the fabrication of CoCrFeNiMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings via coaxial powder-fed laser cladding, addressing porosity and impurity issues in conventional methods. The HEA coatings exhibited eutectic/hypereutectic microstructures under all laser power conditions. A systematic investigation of laser power effects (1750–2500 W) reveals that 2250 W optimizes microstructure and performance, yielding a dual-phase structure with FCC matrix and dispersed σ phases (Fe-Cr/Mo-rich). The coating achieves exceptional hardness (738.3 HV0.2, 3.8× substrate), ultralow wear rate (4.55 × 10−5 mm3/N·m), and minimized corrosion current (2.31 × 10−4 A/cm2) in 3.5 wt.% NaCl. The friction mechanism of the CoCrFeNiMo HEA coating is that in high-speed friction and wear, the oxide film is formed on the surface of the coating, and then the rupture of the oxide film leads to adhesive wear and abrasive wear. The corrosion mechanism is the galvanic corrosion caused by the potential difference between the FCC phase and the σ phase.Keywords: high-entropy alloy coatings, coaxial powder-feeding laser cladding, CoCrFeNiMo, laser power

The CoCrFeNi and CoCrFeNiMn HEA coatings exhibit single-phase FCC structures, while the CoCrFeNiTi coating comprises FCC, Laves, and η phases, and the CoCrFeNiMo coating consists of FCC and σ phases. Among these, the CoCrFeNiMo coating demonstrates the highest hardness (~700 HV) and optimal wear resistance due to σ-phase strengthening, with oxidative wear identified as the dominant wear mechanism. However, the multiphase structures induce galvanic corrosion effects, resulting in comparatively inferior corrosion resistance for both CoCrFeNiMo and CoCrFeNiTi coatings.

Grain boundary decohesion has been recently shown to occur readily for this alloy due to segregation and nanoclustering of Cr, Ni and Mn at elevated temperature, and these failures typically originate along HAGBs and at triple junctions. In the present work there is no significant evidence of grain boundary segregation, and this is reasonable as a negligible increase in temperature is expected for these sliding conditions.
